summary: Defines a credential service that lets SIP user agents discover other users' certificates through a SIP event package, by subscribing to the service for an address-of-record and getting an authenticated response.

eli5.summary: To send a private message to someone, you need their public certificate. This lets a SIP phone ask a server for it.

subtitle: A SIP service that hands out users' certificates, and optionally their private keys, so end-to-end encryption becomes practical.

tldr.problem: SIP can use S/MIME for end-to-end encryption and integrity, but it has not been widely deployed, partly because there is no good way to distribute certificates.
tldr.mechanism: Two new SIP event packages, certificate and credential. A caller subscribes to a person's address-of-record and receives the certificate in a NOTIFY signed by an authentication service (SIP Identity). Users publish and fetch their own certificate and private key over TLS with Digest authentication.
tldr.outcome: Certificates can be self-signed yet strongly bound to a SIP identity. The scheme depends heavily on trusting the credential service and the authentication service.

facts.label: Notification rate
facts.value: No more than once per minute

facts.label: Renewal window
facts.value: notAfter within 600 seconds, random wait of 0 to 300 seconds

today: RFC 6072 is a Proposed Standard (February 2011), and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why SIP Needs Certificate Distribution
sections.content:
RFC 3261, as amended by RFC 3853, provides end-to-end encryption and integrity using S/MIME (RFC 5751). Several security properties in RFC 3261 depend on S/MIME, yet it has not been widely deployed. One reason given is the complexity of providing a reasonable certificate distribution infrastructure.

This specification offers a way to handle discovery, retrieval and management of certificates for SIP. Combined with SIP Identity (RFC 4474), users can have certificates that are not signed by any well-known certification authority while their identity is still strongly bound to the certificate. It also lets SIP user agents such as IP phones enroll and obtain their credentials with no more configuration than they commonly have today.

The document defines a certificate as an X.509 (RFC 5280) certificate with a public key and identities in the SubjectAltName, and a credential as the combination of a certificate and its private key.
sections.eli5: Secret notes between phones were hard to use because nobody had an easy way to get each other's locks. This makes getting a lock easy.

sections.title: The Credential Service
sections.content:
The approach is a new SIP service, the credential service. A user agent (UA) subscribes to another user's certificate using a SIP event package (RFC 3265), and the certificate arrives in a NOTIFY request. An authentication service as in RFC 4474 signs that NOTIFY with the proxy domain's certificate. The authentication service vouches that the sender may use the From address, and the sender vouches that this is an appropriate certificate for that user.

Users can also store and fetch their own credentials, using SIP PUBLISH (RFC 3903) to update them. The UA authenticates with a shared secret, typically the same one it uses for REGISTER, usually with SIP Digest Authentication. The UA first does a TLS handshake (RFC 5246) to be sure it is talking to the right credential server.

The text describes three deployment styles:

  1. The server stores only certificates, and private keys get onto devices some other way.
  2. The server stores certificates and an encrypted private key. It does not know the password phrase, so the user types it on each device.
  3. The server generates and stores certificates and private keys, possibly with unencrypted PKCS #8 objects and no password phrases.

The only way Alice can trust that a certificate is Bob's, and that the NOTIFY was not spoofed, is to check the Identity header field value.

Certificates signed by well-known certification authorities also work, but the text notes that adding SIP URIs to the SubjectAltName has rarely been implemented by commercial authorities. Most UAs would use self-signed certificates plus an authentication service.
sections.eli5: There is a helper office that keeps everyone's locks. You ask it for a friend's lock, and a trusted stamp on the answer shows it is the real one.

sections.title: The certificate Event Package
sections.content:
A UA finds a certificate by sending a SUBSCRIBE with event type certificate to the address-of-record (AOR) it wants. The subscription defines no SUBSCRIBE bodies, and the default duration is one day. Authenticating this subscription is not necessary.

The Notifier MUST immediately send a NOTIFY with the current certificate, or an empty body if none exists. The body is application/pkix-cert with Content-Disposition signal. The NOTIFY's From header field is set to the To value of the SUBSCRIBE, and the NOTIFY must pass through an authentication service, which in turn requires the SUBSCRIBE to have been routed through it.

On receipt, the UA MUST check that the NOTIFY is correctly signed by an authentication service. If the asserted identity does not match the AOR subscribed to, the certificate MUST NOT be used. It is removed from the cache when a NOTIFY with an empty body arrives (revocation) or a new certificate replaces it.

  • Cache time SHOULD be configurable, with a default of one day RECOMMENDED. A UA MUST NOT cache a certificate longer than the subscription duration.
  • Notifiers SHOULD NOT send NOTIFY requests more than once per minute.
  • Forked requests are not permitted, the server MUST be a state agent, and the event list extension MUST NOT be used.
  • If a request using a cached certificate gets a 437 (Unsupported Certificate) response, the UA SHOULD drop it from the cache and fetch it again.
sections.eli5: You ask for a friend's lock and get it right away. If the friend gets a new lock, you are told. You also should not keep an old lock too long in case the news never reached you.

sections.title: The credential Event Package
sections.content:
UAs fetch and store their own credentials with the credential event package. Subscriptions run from hours to one week, with a default of one day. The NOTIFY body is multipart/mixed and holds at least an application/pkix-cert (a DER-encoded X.509v3 certificate) and an application/pkcs8 body (a DER-encoded PrivateKeyInfo). Integrity and confidentiality of the PKCS #8 objects come from TLS.

The UA MUST use TLS to connect directly to the credential service, or to a server authoritative for its domain, and MUST NOT go through an intermediate proxy. It checks that the server certificate matches the expected name, because failing to do so may result in publishing private key material to an attacker. The service MUST challenge the UA with SIP Digest, and only a UA that can authenticate as able to register as that AOR is authorized.

To update credentials the UA sends a PUBLISH with the certificate alone, or a multipart body with both parts. The service checks that the notBefore time is not in the future, the notAfter time is in the future, and any cA basic constraint is FALSE. It SHOULD NOT check the SubjectAltName. A PUBLISH with no body and Expires=0 revokes the credentials, and certificate subscribers then get a NOTIFY with an empty body.

If a credential is revoked, the service MUST terminate current subscriptions with a NOTIFY whose Subscription-State is terminated and reason deactivated, forcing re-authentication. If a UA cannot decrypt the PKCS #8 object, it MUST send a 437 response.
sections.eli5: Your own lock and key can be stored at the helper office too. It will only give them back to you after you show a secret password and talk over a private line.

sections.title: When a UA Makes New Credentials
sections.content:
A UA SHOULD retrieve its credentials after it registers. It generates a new credential when it receives a credential NOTIFY with no body, when its certificate has expired, when the certificate's notAfter date is within the next 600 seconds, or when the user asks to revoke and reissue.

In the 600-second case, the UA waits a random time between 0 and 300 seconds. If no new credentials arrive in that time, it creates replacements and sends them in a PUBLISH. A new key pair needs proper randomness (RFC 4086). The private key MAY be encrypted with a password phrase from the user. To revoke without a replacement, the UA MUST send a PUBLISH with an empty body.

Certificate generation guidance: the signature algorithms sha1WithRSAEncryption and sha256WithRSAEncryption MUST be implemented, the issuer SHOULD be the same as the subject, a validity of one year or less is RECOMMENDED, and the SubjectAltName needs a URI with the user's SIP AOR.
sections.eli5: A little before a lock wears out, the phone waits a random short while and then makes a new one. The random wait stops everyone from changing locks at the same moment.

sections.title: Identity Signature and Crypto Profiles
sections.content:
RFC 4474 defined an authentication service signature called rsa-sha1. This document adds rsa-sha256, computed the same way except with sha256WithRSAEncryption. Implementations MUST implement both, and IANA registered rsa-sha256 in the Identity-Info algorithm parameter registry.

For TLS, credential services MUST support TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA and TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA256, SHOULD implement server name indication, MUST NOT negotiate cipher suites with NULL encryption, integrity or authentication, and clients and servers MUST NOT use SSL 2.0.

For private key protection, clients MUST implement PBES2 with PBKDF2 using HMAC with both SHA-1 and SHA-256, and the encryption algorithm id-aes128-wrap-pad. A different password SHOULD be used for key encryption than for authentication. Some pre-standard deployments used DES-EDE2-CBC-Pad, which may be worth supporting.
sections.eli5: The rules say which kinds of secret codes everyone must know so that any two phones can talk, and which weak codes must never be used.

sections.title: Trust and Security Considerations
sections.content:
To trust a received certificate that is not signed by a trusted authority with a matching name, the UA MUST do all of these things. The NOTIFY's From must match the original URI subscribed to. The Identity header must validate. The certificate validity times must be checked. The certificate must be used only for the identity the authentication service asserted. The memo calls this chain from original URI to From, to body, to public key critical: if any step is skipped, the system will not work.

Revocation. Publishing a new credential notifies subscribers in seconds. Because an attacker could block the NOTIFY, UAs must limit how long they cache certificates, with a default of one day suggested and zero possible.

Single point of trust. The whole scheme depends on trusting the credential service operators, and the security of all users is compromised if it is compromised. A compromised authentication service is described as one of the worst attacks, comparable to a compromised certification authority, since it enables a man-in-the-middle. A UA MAY subscribe to its own certificate under another identity to detect this, or save and show certificate fingerprints.

Private keys should be stored encrypted, ideally using tamper-resistant hardware, on both devices and server.
sections.eli5: The whole thing works only if you trust the helper office and its stamp. If a bad person controlled it, they could hand out fake locks.

messages.note: Sent to Bob's AOR, routed via the proxy and authentication service.
